title: The thirtieth part
hookLine: the surahs you know by heart
tomorrow: Dadi wants the whole book read at home. how fast is too fast?

lines: WHO STARTS A BOOK AT THE END?
cards: A weekend-school recital. A seven-year-old in a tiny white cap walks up to the microphone, takes a huge breath, and recites. Not from the opening pages of the Qur'an.
From the very back. The next child does the same, and the next. Parents film on their phones; somebody's grandmother mouths every word along with them.
And here's the odd thing about the evening: these children are learning the book backward, starting from its last part, the thirtieth. Who starts a book at the end?

teach.h: SIZE: THE SHORT ONES LIVE AT THE BACK.
teach.b: Three answers, and the puzzle solves itself. First, size. For reading, the Qur'an is divided into thirty parts.

The last, called Juz 'Amma after its first word, which means about what, holds a cluster of short surahs. Broadly, the surahs grow shorter toward the end, so the back of the book is where the small ones live. Second, use.
In the prayer, after the Fatiha, people recite a little more of the Qur'an, and these short surahs fit that slot. A child who learns al-Ikhlas this week can pray with it tonight.
And one to tell a friend: in a hadith, the Prophet ﷺ said al-Ikhlas, short as it is, equals a third of the Qur'an. Third, the heart.
Hifz, learning by heart, puts the book where it says it belongs: the Qur'an calls itself clear signs in the hearts of those given knowledge.

teach.h: HEART: EASY TO REMEMBER, IF YOU RETURN.
teach.b: It also says, "in truth We have made the Qur'an easy to remember; but is there any that remembereth?" Easy, and then a question.
Because the Prophet also warned that the Qur'an slips from memory faster than a hobbled camel slips its rope, unless you keep coming back to it. So a surah learned at seven isn't finished at seven.
By heart isn't something you did once. It's something you keep doing.

how: Muslim children often begin memorizing the Qur'an with the short surahs of its last part, Juz 'Amma, and recite them in prayer after the Fatiha; adults keep them by reciting them regularly.

o: the Qur'an's opening chapter, said in prayer
a part of the book read only in Ramadan
the Qur'an's last part, full of short surahs

games.q: what solves the puzzle — tap the pairs.
p: the last part, named for 'about what'
short, yet equal to a third of the Qur'an
how fast memory slips without review

s: the surahs are arranged in the order they were revealed
the order isn't by time; broadly, the surahs grow shorter toward the end.
a hadith says al-Ikhlas equals a third of the Qur'an
once a surah is memorized, it stays put
the Prophet warned it slips away faster than a hobbled camel unless you keep returning (Bukhari 5033).

games.q: a coworker who became Muslim recently knows three short surahs and feels behind. she wants to drop them and start a long one to catch up. what fits today?
o: start the long one; the short surahs are mainly for kids.
keep the three alive in her prayers, and add the next short one slowly.
skip memorizing; reading from a screen does the same job.
games.why: the short surahs are the ones that fit the prayer, and by heart is kept by returning. three kept beats one long one half-held.

practice: Choose one short surah you know, even a few lines; al-Ikhlas works. Say it out loud from memory, slowly, once, and where it catches, look it up and say it again whole.
If you don't know one yet, say its first line in English, in Pickthall's words: "Say: He is Allah, the One!"

wordCard.voice: The thirtieth part: Juz 'Amma, the back of the book, where the short surahs live and where children begin.

orig.note: Arabic: keeping, guarding; learning the Qur'an by heart.

carryVoice: Carry this: by heart, which means kept, because you keep coming back to it. Four of fifteen, and the view is opening.
